title: Dixieland as a fashionable fad and its decline
summary: Dixieland had seasons of popularity; society crowds came for fashion, now less so.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: What do you think now about the future of this music now? I don't know. Dix-Land. Oh, Dix-Land.

Well, Dix-Land never has died, of course, very well. And, but it has seasons of popularity. It got to be the end thing to do, you know, whether or not, how many times these people would come in with the mink coat. And I didn't know a bass drum from a cannon, but sometimes it sounded like. But we'd come in here and it was a thing to do, it was to go to dinner at Antwine's or Brennan's and we'll listen to some Dix-Land. And then you tell your social life friends, I went down and I heard some Dix-Land. It was a thing to do, it was a fashionable thing to do, and it rolled along for many years like that because of that, not completely because of that altogether, but because that played a big part of it. Which wasn't a bad thing to subject these people to some music, you know, well, good gracious. And, but they didn't know what they were listening to, most of them, but again and again, but then again, there were the people that did know. But for the most part, it was a fashionable thing to do, it was like, so you get a little television exposure, we must go down and see you. Whether we appreciate really or know really what you're putting down, we must go see you because we saw you on television.
Do you think that that, do you think that that has changed now?

That's not so much the end thing to do anymore, I don't know, it's, um, well, uh, I guess it's not, it's not as fast, well, it's fast, but let me get away from that, it's not as popular as it was, let's put it that way. Because after dinner on the street, these little three jazz places would be jam-packed, you just couldn't get in there. People would come in for their drink and clap their hands and stomp their feet a little while and listen to some music and then they'd go home. But they'd do it again next week and the next week and I'd see the same people on a Friday and Saturday and just like clockwork. But now it's, they've gotten away from that a little bit. But everything must change and it's a gradual process.
